Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath

Memory.value: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I have to be on guard all the time

vignette: Kwame Okafor stood at the nurses' station, his stethoscope cool against his chest, waiting for the next page. At twenty, he was already navigating the rigorous rhythm of an urban teaching hospital, but the past few months had quietly reoriented his attention. During a deployment in a dusty theater, a mortar strike had sent a shockwave through a narrow supply corridor. The blast had thrown him against a metal cabinet, and for a long moment, his lungs had fought to draw air through the grit and the weight of his gear. He remembered the sudden absence of sound-the radio chatter cutting out, the wind dropping, a heavy, muffled quiet settling over the compound-before the sharp crack of small-arms fire erupted. In that same heartbeat, a teammate had gone down with a violent, tearing wound, and Kwame had moved, not with thought, but with reflex, engaging the threat before his mind could fully catch up. Now, the hospital floor felt like a continuation of that corridor. When a patient's oxygen line disconnected with a soft hiss, Kwame's breath caught, a familiar tightness climbing his throat until it felt impossible to draw a full breath. He had come to believe that the air itself could turn against him, and he learned to brace for it, counting the seconds until the sensation passed. He noticed this most clearly during night rounds, when the ward slipped into an unexpected silence after a nurse stepped out and the monitors hummed in low, steady registers. That sudden silence made his shoulders tighten; he was certain he was back in the compound, waiting for the next round. He had also learned to scan every doorway, every shifting shadow, his body perpetually braced as if expecting a sudden movement or a sharp sound. What frightened him most was not the noise itself, but the unpredictable violence of it-the way a dropped chart or a raised voice could instantly summon the memory of torn fabric and blood. His mind, however, refused to hold the event together. He pushed the memory away just as it began to surface, like a stone sliding back under water before he could name it. His recall came in disconnected pieces: the scuff of a boot on concrete, a flash of daylight behind a tarp, the taste of copper, a fragment of a shout that offered no context. There were long stretches of the deployment he simply could not remember, no matter how hard he tried to force them forward; the timeline had torn away in places, leaving him with gaps he could not stitch. In these moments, Kwame felt unmoored from his own identity. He looked at his white coat, at the steady hands that sutured and listened, and wondered if the doctor was merely a costume worn over someone who no longer recognized his own reflection. His beliefs about how the world operated-about predictability, about safety, about the steady rhythm of daily life-had been completely shattered, and he navigated the clinic floor with a quiet, continuous assessment of every threat. Over the months, his avoidance had taken root in the routine. He began skipping the quiet reading room, preferring the constant noise of the main ward where sounds were evenly distributed. He declined invitations to group dinners, finding the sudden laughter and shifting chairs too jarring. The consequences accumulated steadily: he missed a departmental briefing because he had waited out a period of sudden silence in the parking lot, and his attending had noted the absent chair without comment. A PCL-5 score of 63 had formalized what his days had already proven, but it was the mounting weight of unexplained tension that finally pushed him to schedule an intake. Now, standing at the station with his breath steady but his gaze fixed on the corridor, Kwame was ready to step into a therapist's office. He hoped to find a way to let the memory surface without pushing it away, and to finally know himself again beneath the constant vigilance.
